source.title: Some Open Problems in Topological Algebra

accepted.question_text: Does every topological group arise as a quotient group of a zero-dimensional topological group of the same weight, and more specifically, under what conditions is an almost metrizable topological group a quotient of a zero-dimensional group of the same weight? Here a space X is zero-dimensional when dim X = 0, and a topological group is almost metrizable when it contains a compact subset of countable character.

evidence.quote:
Problem 1 (Choban). Is every topological group a quotient group of a zero-dimensional topological group of the same weight? When an almost metrizable topological group is a quotient of a zero-dimensional group of the same weight?
A space X is zero-dimensional if dim X = 0. A topological group is almost metrizable if contains a compact subset of countable character.

accepted.question_text: Under which conditions is the free universal algebra of an uncountable signature over a metrizable space X paracompact, and in particular, is the free topological linear space L(X) over X, taken over the discrete field of real numbers, paracompact?

evidence.quote: Problem 2 (Choban). Under which conditions is the free universal algebra of an uncountable signature over a metrizable space X paracompact? In particular, is the free topological linear space L(X) of X over the discrete field of real numbers paracompact?

accepted.question_text: For a zero-dimensional compact homogeneous space X, is the semigroup S(X) of all continuous self-maps of X, equipped with the topology of pointwise convergence inherited from the product X^X, left bounded? Here a semigroup with identity e is left bounded if for every neighborhood U of e there is a finite subset F such that S = FU, and a space X is homogeneous if any two points of X are related by a homeomorphism of X.

evidence.quote:
A semigroup S with the identity e endowed with a topology is called a left (resp. right) bounded if for every neighborhood U of e there is a finite subset F of S such that S = F U (resp. S = UF); S is called bounded if S is both left and right bounded.
For a topological space X let S(X) ⊂ XX be the semigroup of all continuous self-mappings of X endowed with the topology of pointwise convergence (i.e., the topology inherited from the Tychonov product XX). A topological space X is called homogeneous if for any points x1, x2 ∈ X there is a homemorphism h of X with h(x1) = x2.
Problem 3 (Protasov). Is the semigroup S(X) left bounded for every zero-dimensional compact homogeneous space?

accepted.question_text: For a zero-dimensional homogeneous space X, is the semigroup S(X) of all continuous self-maps of X, with the topology of pointwise convergence, right bounded? Here right bounded means that for every neighborhood U of the identity there is a finite subset F such that S(X) = U F.

evidence.quote: Problem 4 (Protasov). Is the semigroup S(X) right bounded for any zero-dimensional homogeneous space X?

accepted.question_text: Let X be a compact space and let H be a distal subgroup of S(X) that acts transitively on X. Must H be left bounded? Here S(X) is the semigroup of continuous self-maps of X, and a subgroup H is distal if for any distinct points x1, x2 in X and any point x in X there exists a neighborhood U of x such that {h(x1), h(x2)} is not contained in U for every h in H.

evidence.quote:
A subgroup H of S(X) is called distal if for any distinct points x1, x2 ∈ X and any point x ∈ X there is a neighborhood U of x such that {h(x1), h(x2)} 6⊂ U for all h ∈ H. It is proven in [11, Theorem 4] that a left bounded subgroup H ⊂ S(X) is distal provided H acts transitively on X.
Problem 5 (Protasov). Let X be a compact space and H be a distal subgroup of S(X), acting transitively on X. Is H left bounded?

accepted.question_text: If G is a bounded semitopological group, or more generally a bounded quasitopological group, must G have countable cellularity? Here a semitopological group is a group whose topology is invariant under both left and right shifts, a quasitopological group is a semitopological group with continuous inversion, and bounded means both left bounded and right bounded.

evidence.quote: Problem 6 (Protasov). Let G be a bounded semitopological (quasitopological) group. Has G countable cellularity?

accepted.question_text: Does every zero-dimensional compact homogeneous space admit the structure of a left topological group, and in particular, if K is a first-countable zero-dimensional compact space, does its countable power K^ω admit the structure of a left topological group? The source also states that this problem had already been answered negatively by Banakh for a homogeneous first-countable zero-dimensional compactum.

evidence.quote: Problem 7 (Protasov). Does every zero-dimensional compact homogeneous space admit the structure of a left topological group?1 In particular, does the countable power Kω of a first-countable zero-dimensional compact space K admit the structure of a left topological group?
1This problem was answered in negative by Banakh in [T.Banakh, A homogeneous first-countable zero-dimensional compactum failing to be a left-topological group, Mat. Stud.29 (2008) 215–217].

accepted.question_text: Does every compact left topological group G support a strictly positive probability Borel measure, meaning a Borel probability measure μ such that μ(U) > 0 for every nonempty open subset U of G?
accepted.context_brief: Measures on compact left topological groups

evidence.quote: Problem 8 (Protasov). Does every compact left topological group G support a strictly positive probability Borel measure?

accepted.question_text: Can every non-discrete topological group G be algebraically generated by a nowhere dense subset?

evidence.quote: Problem 9 (Protasov). Can every non-discrete topological group G be algebraically generated by a nowhere dense subset?2

accepted.question_text: If a paratopological group G is right ω-bounded, must it also be left ω-bounded? Here G is left ω-bounded if for every neighborhood U of the origin there exists a countable subset F of G such that G = F U, and right ω-bounded if for every neighborhood U there exists a countable subset F with G = U F.

evidence.quote:
A paratopological group G is left ω-bounded (resp. right ω-bounded) if for any neighborhood U ⊂ G of the origin there is a countable subset F ⊂ G with G = F U (resp. G = UF); G is ω-bounded if it is both left and right ω-bounded.
Problem 10 (Guran). Is a paratopological group G left ω-bounded if it is right ω-bounded?

accepted.question_text: Is there a metrizable o-bounded topological group G such that player I has a winning strategy in the game OF(G)? Here a subset A of a topological group G is o-bounded if for every sequence (U_n) of neighborhoods of the origin there exists a sequence of finite sets (F_n) such that A is contained in the union of F_n U_n, and in the game OF(A), player I chooses neighborhoods U_n while player II chooses finite sets F_n, with player II winning when A is contained in the union of F_n U_n.

evidence.quote:
A subset A of a topological group G is called o-bounded if for any sequence (Un)n∈ω of neighborhoods of the origin of G there is a sequence (Fn)n∈ω of finite subsets of G such that A ⊂ S n∈ω FnUn. ... Next, given a subset A of a topological group G, consider the following game OF(A) (abbreviated from Open-Finite). Two players, I and II, choose at every step k ∈ ω a neighborhood Un ⊂ G of the origin, and a finite subset Fn of G, respectively. At the end of the game, the player II is declared the winner if A ⊂ S n∈ω FnUn. ...
Problem 11 (Banakh). Is there a (metrizable) o-bounded topological group G such that the player I has a winning strategy in the game OF(G)?

accepted.question_text: Let A be a compact subset of the real line R such that the difference set A − A = {a − a′ : a, a′ ∈ A} is a neighborhood of 0 in R. Must the fourfold sumset A + A + A + A have non-empty interior in R?
accepted.context_brief: Additive structure of compact subsets of R

evidence.quote: Problem 12 (Banakh). Let A be a compact subset of the real line R such that A − A = {a−a′ : a, a′ ∈ A} is a neighborhood of zero in R. Has the sum A+A+A+A non-empty interior in R?
